items.claim: Liberals exhibit low vaccine hesitancy and high booster uptake rates regardless of the political climate of their region.
Conservatives living in liberal political climates have lower vaccine hesitancy and higher booster uptake rates than conservatives living in conservative political climates.
The interaction between political conservatism and regional climate was not significant for initial vaccine status, unlike for hesitancy and booster status.
The authors extend the existing literature by combining the previously separate lines of research on individual political orientation and regional political climate to examine their interaction.

The paper investigates how partisan polarization varied geographically and temporally during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States and Canada, specifically examining the impact of public health interventions and political events.

Politically conservative regions in both the US and Canada exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization regarding COVID-19 topics, with a strong negative correlation between vaccine polarization and vaccination rates in the US, though this relationship was weaker or absent in Canada.

The paper investigates whether Democratic Party messaging that labels Donald Trump as a 'convicted criminal' causes negative spillover effects on Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records more broadly, and whether a counter-narrative featuring a formerly system-involved representative can mitigate these effects.

Exposure to a Democratic Party advertisement labeling Trump as a 'convicted criminal' significantly worsens Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records, but this negative effect is largely ameliorated when participants are first exposed to a counter-narrative featuring the perspective of a formerly incarcerated state representative.

The negative impact of the Trump advertisement on perceptions of individuals with criminal records was more pronounced for participants who identified as being system-impacted compared to those who did not.

The authors position their work within social categorization theory, using it to explain how the salience of Trump as a 'convicted criminal' exemplar leads to homogenized spillover perceptions of individuals with records, and they extend this by testing perspective-getting interventions to mitigate these effects.

The paper disputes or builds on the claim that negative campaign advertisements effectively aid election success, noting that meta-analytic evidence does not empirically support this use, and that Democrats tend to respond more to positive ads than Republicans.
The study uses a dataset combining panel survey data and behavioral data from X/Twitter for American users between 2019 and 2021, employing cross-sectional, panel, and exploratory count models.
